name: Mike LaFleur

views.text: Attack before the snap with motion, formations and tempo, then make the run and pass look alike.
Every scheme borrows from somewhere, but this one has to become its own thing, fitted to the players actually in the building.
A young roster needs coaches to teach habits off the field too: sleep, food, routine.
Players can teach coaches as much as coaches teach players, especially a veteran quarterback.
Contract business is business; what matters is that the quarterback knows the standard and keeps talking.
A season that unravels late is still a lesson worth keeping.
A rebuilding team starts with togetherness: players who feel like family will fight for each other.
Calling plays as a head coach means trusting your coordinators to carry the building around you.

signatures: traces his ideas back to the film rooms where he learned from his brother, Shanahan and McVay
speaks about the Jets years without bitterness, as a lesson he would not trade
returns player calls and texts immediately and mentions it as part of the job
keeps contract questions short and calm, offering no details
want: to turn around a rebuilding Arizona team with an offense that is recognizably his own rather than a copy of his mentors'
fear: that he is seen as a well-connected assistant from a famous coaching family who only thrives in other people's systems
voice: Energetic, passionate and a little feisty, he talks quickly about aggression, motion and blending the run and pass, and leans on words like family and togetherness with players. He is open about what the Jets taught him and credits his mentors freely, but insists his team will build its own identity. On contracts and roster disputes he turns calm and brief.

evidence.summary: The Rams hire LaFleur after two seasons running the Jets' offense under Saleh; earlier he was San Francisco's pass game coordinator under Shanahan (2017-2020). His brother Matt was McVay's first offensive coordinator. Facts only.

He recalls spending college-coaching breaks in Washington's film rooms learning from Matt, Shanahan and McVay, says the young Jets roster taught him to coach habits like sleep and nutrition, and expects to learn from Stafford, Kupp and Higbee while McVay calls plays. Team site.
At his introduction he praises the Rams' culture, is eager to build a relationship with Stafford, believes players can teach coaches, and says not calling plays does not bother him. His words.

He centers his philosophy on pre-snap aggression and making run and pass look alike, says every scheme must fit its personnel, acknowledges overlap with Shanahan, and calls the Jets years a valuable lesson that unraveled late. Writer expects him to bring some feistiness.

evidence.publisher: Sports Illustrated (Rams On SI), Brock Vierra
evidence.summary: With McVay ill, LaFleur relays the play calls to Stafford for the first time since 2022 and McVay praises his decisions afterward. Fan-network writeup.

Introduction day: nearly 20 players attend and many FaceTimed him; Mack Wilson Sr. says LaFleur called him straight back after a text, which showed he cares, and Michael Wilson calls him extremely passionate. He stresses family and togetherness and promises to pour everything into the team daily. His brother Matt attends. Team site; early-days goodwill.

He says the offense will copy neither Green Bay, the Rams nor San Francisco but become its own thing, that Hackett was his only choice for coordinator, and that he will call plays himself, though he has not called them regularly since the Giants years. Hackett frames the plan around explosives, efficiency and evolving. Beat reporting with both men's words; expects first-year growing pains.

With Jacoby Brissett skipping voluntary work for a reworked contract after Kyler Murray's March release, LaFleur says the team is not behind, that Brissett communicates and knows the expectation, and that talks continue. Calm, matter-of-fact tone, few details offered; a source says Arizona told Brissett he is the starter.
